Props to Gustavo Ourique, the undergrad who discovered Dox's spectrum after culling visually through nearly 300 000 spectral graphs. For me though, I don't even understand how is stuff like this even figured out.

It's actually really easy! The term is astronomical spectroscopy. Essentially analyzing the light emitted from a distant hot body (like a star) can tell you an enormous about it from its temperature to its chemical composition. The chemical composition part comes down in the end it literally looking at a breakdown of the color spectrum emitted from the body. There will be little slices missing and these slices correspond to various elements. Helium, for instance, was discovered through this method on another body (and named) before being discovered on Earth! So something that's pure oxygen would be missing only the bar that corresponds to oxygen.

We've been doing this for centuries, but only very recently understood why it works and that is vastly more complex and all the information we have was only causally connected in the early 20th century and gets into quantum mechanical interactions and all other sorts of fun stuff, but just knowing what we do is pretty easy!
